retrogroup

Patient-level survival outcomes for a whole clinical trial are frequently available alongside published subgroup hazard ratios, while the subgroup membership of each patient is not. retrogroup reconstructs subgroup membership from these two sources of information. A Bayesian survival model estimates the posterior probability that each patient belongs to each subgroup level, and a sampling method uses these probabilities to impute a subgroup level for each patient.

Installation

To install the latest release version of retrogroup, open R and run:

install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("wlandau/retrogroup@*release")

To install the development version of retrogroup:

pak::pak("wlandau/retrogroup")

Usage

A typical workflow has four steps: gather the patient-level data and the published subgroup statistics, convert them to the standard format of retrogroup, sample subgroup membership for each patient, and optionally optimize the sampled subgroups to match the published statistics.

Example data

The example below uses the colon dataset from the survival package, which comes from the adjuvant colon cancer trial of levamisole plus fluorouracil (Moertel et al., 1990). group_example_patient() returns the patient-level survival data, with no subgroup information:

library(retrogroup)
group_example_patient()
#> # A tibble: 619 × 3
#>    arm      time event
#>    <chr>   <dbl> <int>
#>  1 Lev+5FU  1521     1
#>  2 Lev+5FU  3087     0
#>  3 Obs       963     1
#>  4 Lev+5FU   293     1
#>  5 Obs       659     1
#>  6 Lev+5FU  1767     1
#>  7 Obs      3192     0
#>  8 Lev+5FU  3308     0
#>  9 Lev+5FU  3309     0
#> 10 Obs      2085     1
#> # ℹ 609 more rows

group_example_summary() returns subgroup statistics like the ones a publication would report. For each level of age, nodal status, and sex, it gives the number of patients and the log hazard ratio (with standard error) of treatment versus control.

group_example_summary()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   variable level      patients log_hazard_ratio standard_error
#>   <chr>    <chr>         <int>            <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 age      under 60        280           -0.169          0.178
#> 2 age      60 or over      339           -0.546          0.160
#> 3 node4    no              453           -0.417          0.153
#> 4 node4    yes             166           -0.312          0.190
#> 5 sex      female          312           -0.147          0.162
#> 6 sex      male            307           -0.656          0.179

Pre-processing

group_data_patient() and group_data_summary() check the input data for consistency and convert it to the standard format the rest of the package expects. You supply the column names of your own data and state which study arm is the treatment arm.

patient <- group_data_patient(
  group_example_patient(),
  arm = "arm",
  treatment = "Lev+5FU",
  time = "time",
  event = "event"
)

summary <- group_data_summary(
  group_example_summary(),
  variable = "variable",
  level = "level",
  patients = "patients",
  log_hazard_ratio = "log_hazard_ratio",
  standard_error = "standard_error"
)

Sampling

group_sample_unconstrained() estimates1 the posterior probability that each patient belongs to each subgroup level, then samples a subgroup level independently for each patient. group_sample_constrained() is similar, but it ensures that the number of patients in each subgroup level exactly matches the respective count in summary$patients.

set.seed(0)
sample <- group_sample_constrained(patient, summary)
sample
#> # A tibble: 619 × 6
#>    treatment  time event age        node4 sex   
#>        <int> <dbl> <int> <fct>      <fct> <fct> 
#>  1         1  1521     1 60 or over no    male  
#>  2         1  3087     0 under 60   yes   female
#>  3         0   963     1 under 60   no    male  
#>  4         1   293     1 60 or over no    male  
#>  5         0   659     1 60 or over no    male  
#>  6         1  1767     1 under 60   no    male  
#>  7         0  3192     0 60 or over yes   female
#>  8         1  3308     0 60 or over no    female
#>  9         1  3309     0 60 or over no    male  
#> 10         0  2085     1 60 or over no    female
#> # ℹ 609 more rows

Each sampled dataset is one random draw, so its subgroup hazard ratios differ somewhat from the published ones. Across many draws, however, they match the published log hazard ratios on average. The sampling benchmarks show this for both the colon cancer example and simulated data.

Optimization

Optimization refines a single sampled dataset so that its subgroup hazard ratios match the published ones. group_optimize_unconstrained() starts from the output of group_sample_unconstrained() and moves one patient at a time to the subgroup level that best reduces the discrepancy. group_optimize_constrained() starts from the output of group_sample_constrained() and swaps the subgroup levels of pairs of patients, so the number of patients in each subgroup level never changes.

set.seed(0)
optimized <- group_optimize_constrained(
  sample,
  summary,
  iterations = 10000L,
  tolerance = 4e-5
)

group_analysis_summary() computes the subgroup statistics of a patient-level dataset.

group_analysis_summary(optimized)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   variable level      patients log_hazard_ratio standard_error
#>   <chr>    <chr>         <int>            <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 age      under 60        280           -0.168          0.174
#> 2 age      60 or over      339           -0.545          0.163
#> 3 node4    no              453           -0.416          0.150
#> 4 node4    yes             166           -0.314          0.195
#> 5 sex      female          312           -0.149          0.158
#> 6 sex      male            307           -0.656          0.183

The optimized dataset matches the published counts, log hazard ratios, and standard errors in summary.

summary
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   variable level      patients log_hazard_ratio standard_error
#>   <chr>    <chr>         <int>            <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 age      under 60        280           -0.169          0.178
#> 2 age      60 or over      339           -0.546          0.160
#> 3 node4    no              453           -0.417          0.153
#> 4 node4    yes             166           -0.312          0.190
#> 5 sex      female          312           -0.147          0.162
#> 6 sex      male            307           -0.656          0.179

See Optimizing subgroup levels for the method and the optimization benchmarks for its performance.
